rv.q: There is still terrific acting and writing, reminding us that some of our problems, as human beings, can be solved only by compassion, not politics.
Penhall’s play makes the case for more care and empathy.
It could be a play of the last 14 years, every character bearing the brunt of a system that is broken, under-resourced and failing the nation.
My lasting impression from The Constituent is the reminder that James Corden has been away too long.
My key reservation is that given how militant ideologues now swirl around our MPs, rogue fathers seem a soft target.
Where ‘The Constituent’ unfortunately goes off the rails is in the introduction of a third character.
Penhall’s dialogue is packed with zap and zing … the performances are pretty much faultless … the play is at once too narrow and too broad
But the surprisingly thin play squanders both its timely subject matter and the talents of the cast.
In a cynical world, Penhall’s play is notable for its empathy – a quality that Monica strives for, and which is baked into the show at a fundamental level.
This production is a timely reminder of the fact that some MPs literally put their lives on the line to do a job that many feel is a duty and a privilege.
The cumulative effect becomes more frustration than fascination.
Corden is outstanding, however, and the manic energy that turbo charged the comedy of One Man is here repurposed in a more dramatic context.
Joe Penhall's script is full of jokes that don't land and the set up is clunky and hard to believe.

cn.t: Corden delivers a strong dramatic performance opposite Maxwell Martin in Penhall's timely political two-hander, though critics find the script itself surprisingly thin and underdeveloped despite sharp moments and relevant themes.
